Build plan

From ordering parts to a robot that rears up on its own: seven milestones, each with a test that tells you it worked.

On this page

  2. Milestone 1: drives on its tail
  3. Milestone 2: PID balance
  4. Milestone 3: policy in simulation
  5. Milestone 4: policy on the robot
  6. Milestone 5: policy on board
  7. Milestone 6: head
Read this first: AI-generated, not yet builtThis design, its code and these pages were generated with AI, and nobody has built or tested a physical Tailwhip yet. The CAD, simulator, trained policy, firmware and print files are complete and checked numerically, and every performance number here comes from simulation. Treat it as a well-worked starting point: measure the parts the pages tell you to, check each step as you go, expect to fix things, and build at your own risk, especially around the 18650 cells. The Limits page lists what to measure and watch.

Seven milestones, in order. Each ends with a test; don't move on until it passes. Times are estimates for someone who has soldered and 3D printed before.

# Milestone Time Passes when
0 Order, measure, print, bench test 1-2 weeks of waiting, 2 evenings of work Every sensor and actuator works from the laptop; the bench measurements are in host/measurements.json
1 Drives on its tail 1 evening Driven by keyboard while resting on its tail, 2 m forward and back, turns both ways
2 PID balance 1-2 evenings Placed upright by hand, it balances for 60 s and drifts less than 1 m
3 Policy in simulation 1 hour (mostly waiting) The policy you trained rears up, balances and survives shoves across the randomised robots
4 Policy on the robot 1-3 evenings It rears up by itself 8 times in 10, balances 60 s, and survives a shove that knocks the PID over
5 Policy on board 1 evening The same, with the laptop unplugged
6 Head 1 evening The ESP32-CAM streams video while it balances, and turning the head doesn't upset it

Milestone 0: order, measure, print, bench test

  1. Order the parts on the Parts page. If you don't have them already: TT motors with wheels, SG-90s (or MG90S), an MPU6050, two ESP32 dev boards, an MX1508, two Mini360 bucks, a 2S protection board, a 2 x 18650 holder, and two good 18650 cells.
  2. Install the software. Arduino IDE with the ESP32 core, and Python 3.10+: bash python -m venv ~/.venvs/tailwhip ~/.venvs/tailwhip/bin/pip install mujoco gymnasium stable-baselines3 numpy manifold3d trimesh pyserial
  3. Train the policy now, while you wait for parts (milestone 3 below). It takes about an hour on a laptop and you'll want it later.
  4. Measure before you print. Calipers on one TT motor and one wheel: the five numbers listed under "Before you print" on the Mechanical page. Edit them in cad/tailwhip.py and run python cad/analysis.py && python cad/export.py. Every check in cad/out/analysis.md should still say PASS.
  5. Print core_left first and check that a TT motor sits on its bosses with the bolt holes lined up. Then print the rest (print settings on the Mechanical page). The tail is ABS.
  6. Build the power system on the bench, without the robot: cells, holder, protection board, fuse, switch, the two Mini360s set to 5.0 V with a meter before anything is connected to them. The Electronics page walks through it with a meter check at every step.
  7. Flash both ESP32s (robot and bridge) and run firmware/i2c_scan first to see the MPU6050 at 0x68.
  8. Assemble the robot (Mechanical page, Assembly), wire it (Electronics page, wiring table).
  9. Bench test from the laptop: python host/bench.py PORT ... has one subcommand per actuator and sensor and one per measurement. Run them all; they write host/measurements.json, which the simulator reads.

Check: both wheels spin both ways, the tail and head sweep, the IMU pitch follows your hand, the IR sensors count edges when you turn the wheels, the battery voltage reads within 0.1 V of your meter, and measurements.json has no empty fields.

Milestone 1: drives on its tail

Set it down on its tail and run python host/drive.py PORT. Arrow keys drive; the tail stays at the rest angle.

Check: 2 m forward and back and turns both ways without tipping. If it pulls to one side, the motors differ: note it, the simulator randomises motor strength by 25 % for exactly this reason.

Milestone 2: PID balance

Switch to pid mode and hold the robot upright, then let go. Start from the gains in docs/software.md and tune them in the order given there.

Check: 60 s upright, less than 1 m of drift with the wheel sensors plugged in. Then unplug the IR sensors and check it still balances (it will drift more). This is the baseline the policy has to beat.

Milestone 3: policy in simulation

python sim/train.py               # about 45 minutes on a 10-core laptop; tensorboard --logdir sim/runs to watch
python sim/evaluate.py            # scores it over 50 randomised robots per test
python sim/demo.py                # films the whole act to sim/out/demo.mp4

If you ran the bench measurements first, the simulator's nominal robot is your robot.

Check: evaluate.py rears up and balances in nearly every randomised robot, and the demo video looks like the one on the Overview. The Simulation and RL page has the numbers to compare against.

Milestone 4: policy on the robot

python host/run_policy.py PORT                       # policy runs on the laptop, robot in 'remote' mode

Start with the robot on its tail and give the stand command. Keep a hand near it the first few times.

Check: rears up by itself 8 times in 10, balances 60 s, and survives a shove (a push on the battery sleeve) that makes the PID version fall. If it twitches or rocks where the simulator was calm, measure the radio delay and the backlash again, update measurements.json, retrain from the current policy with python sim/train.py --init sim/policies/tailwhip.zip --steps 5000000 and try again. That loop is the core of sim-to-real.

Milestone 5: policy on board

python sim/export_policy.py       # writes firmware/tailwhip_robot/policy.h (about 30 KB of flash)

Reflash the robot, unplug the laptop, and switch to onboard mode with the switch sequence in docs/software.md.

Check: the same as milestone 4, with no laptop.

Milestone 6: head

Fit the ESP32-CAM in the head (its own 5 V, from the logic buck, or a third Mini360 if it browns out) and flash the stock camera web server example. Pan the head with the head command while it balances.

Check: video streams while it balances, and a full pan doesn't knock it over.

Tailwhip is an open robot project from BuildRobotz. The design was generated with AI and has not yet been built or tested on hardware; performance figures are MuJoCo simulation results. Build at your own risk. Code, CAD and firmware: github.com/buildrobotz/tailwhip-robot (code MIT, docs and CAD CC BY-SA 4.0).
